props.title: The Hearst and Davies Affair

sections.content: **The Hearst and Davies Affair** (1985) offers a fascinating glimpse into one of Hollywood's most notorious relationships, starring Robert Mitchum as newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst and Virginia Madsen as actress Marion Davies. The film directly connects to the inspiration behind Citizen Kane (1941), Orson Welles' masterpiece that thinly veiled its portrayal of Hearst through Charles Foster Kane. While not as cinematically revolutionary as Welles' film, this made-for-television drama captures the extravagant lifestyle and complex power dynamics of 1920s and 1930s Hollywood.

sections.content: The film fits into a broader category of Hollywood-on-Hollywood productions that examine the golden age of cinema. Like **Sunset Boulevard** (1950) and **The Bad and the Beautiful** (1952), it peels back the glamorous facade to reveal the complex power structures and relationships that defined early Hollywood. The portrayal of Davies is particularly noteworthy, as it helps rehabilitate her image from the unfair caricature presented in Citizen Kane (1941), showing her as a talented comedic actress whose career was actually hindered by Hearst's insistence on casting her in serious dramatic roles.

Director David Lowell Rich tackles the 32-year relationship between Hearst and Davies with a focus on the personal rather than the political, distinguishing it from other Hearst-inspired works. While Citizen Kane (1941) emphasized the newspaper magnate's public power and influence, **The Hearst and Davies Affair** (1985) examines the private man and his genuine devotion to Davies, despite remaining married to his first wife Millicent until his death. sections.content: The film belongs to a wave of productions that attempted to demystify Hollywood's golden age. Like **Frances** (1982) and **The Aviator** (2004), it explores the intersection of power, celebrity, and personal relationships in early Hollywood. The production values may reflect its television budget, but Mitchum's nuanced performance as Hearst captures both the mogul's imposing presence and his private vulnerabilities.
